---
title: "Aggregating and Consuming"
---

# Aggregating and Consuming

A consumer calls `next` until it is done and produces a value that is not an iterator. After a consumer runs, the iterator is used up.

## The concept

`collect` builds a collection. The target type decides the shape. `fold` walks every item with an explicit accumulator. `reduce` is `fold` without a starting value, so an empty iterator returns `None`. `sum` and `count` are special cases. `any` and `all` may stop early. `for_each` is a `for` loop written as a method, including the side effects.

## Recipe 23 — Collecting into different container types

`collect` uses `FromIterator`. Name the target when the compiler cannot infer it.

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet};

    let names = ["ada", "linus", "ada"];

    let list: Vec<&str> = names.into_iter().collect();
    assert_eq!(list, ["ada", "linus", "ada"]);

    let unique: HashSet<&str> = names.into_iter().collect();
    assert!(unique.contains("ada") && unique.contains("linus"));
    assert_eq!(unique.len(), 2);

    let lengths: HashMap<&str, usize> = names.into_iter().map(|name| (name, name.len())).collect();
    assert_eq!(lengths.get("linus"), Some(&5));
    assert_eq!(lengths.len(), 2);
}
```

The `HashMap` keeps one entry per key. A later pair with the same key replaces the earlier value. `ada` appears twice, both times with length 3, so the map has two keys.

`collect` into `String` works when the items are `char`:

```rust
fn main() {
    let word: String = ['r', 'u', 's', 't'].into_iter().collect();
    assert_eq!(word, "rust");
}
```

## Recipe 24 — Reducing to a single value with fold()

`fold` takes a starting accumulator and a closure of `(acc, item) -> acc`.

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [10, 20, 30];
    let total = readings.iter().fold(0, |acc, n| acc + n);
    assert_eq!(total, 60);

    let longest = ["ada", "linus", "grace"].iter().fold("", |best, name| {
        if name.len() > best.len() { name } else { best }
    });
    assert_eq!(longest, "linus");
}
```

The start value is returned unchanged when the iterator is empty. That is why `fold` does not return `Option`.

## Recipe 25 — Using reduce() when no initial value is needed

`reduce` uses the first item as the starting accumulator. An empty iterator returns `None`.

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [10, 20, 30];
    let total = readings.into_iter().reduce(|acc, n| acc + n);
    assert_eq!(total, Some(60));

    let empty: [i32; 0] = [];
    assert_eq!(empty.into_iter().reduce(|acc, n| acc + n), None);
}
```

Use `fold` when "empty" has a defined answer (`0` for a sum, `""` for a join you are building by hand). Use `reduce` when an empty input is a different situation from a real total.

## Recipe 26 — Summing and counting

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [10, 20, 30];
    let total: i32 = readings.iter().sum();
    let n = readings.iter().count();
    assert_eq!(total, 60);
    assert_eq!(n, 3);

    let wide: i64 = readings.iter().map(|n| i64::from(*n)).sum();
    assert_eq!(wide, 60);
}
```

`sum` needs a type that implements `Sum`. If inference fails, write `sum::<i32>()`. `count` walks the iterator. On a slice iterator it is cheap, but it still consumes the iterator. Call `len` on the slice when you still need the items afterwards.

## Recipe 27 — Short-circuiting checks with any() and all()

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::cell::Cell;

    let seen = Cell::new(0);
    let readings = [1, 2, 30, 4];
    let has_spike = readings.iter().any(|n| {
        seen.set(seen.get() + 1);
        *n > 10
    });
    assert!(has_spike);
    assert_eq!(seen.get(), 3);

    let all_positive = readings.iter().all(|n| *n > 0);
    assert!(all_positive);

    let none_negative = readings.iter().all(|n| *n >= 0);
    assert!(none_negative);
}
```

`any` stopped at `30` and never looked at `4`. `all` stops at the first failure. On an empty iterator, `any` is `false` and `all` is `true`.

## Recipe 28 — Consuming for side effects with for_each()

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [18, 21, 19];
    let mut hot = Vec::new();
    readings.iter().filter(|n| **n >= 20).for_each(|n| hot.push(*n));
    assert_eq!(hot, [21]);
}
```

`for_each` takes `FnMut(Item)`. A `for` loop is the same control flow and is easier to `break` from. `for_each` cannot `break` or `return` from the enclosing function. Use it at the end of a chain when the chain is the point and the body is one call. Use `for` when the body is a block.
